name: Running a Tailoring and Fashion Business
objectives: Given your own sewing space, machine and tools, check a sewing workshop for safety risks from needles, scissors, irons, electricity and fire, and fix them, finding and fixing at least three risks

Given a customer who wants a garment made, take the customer's measurements and fill in an order card with style, fabric, price, deposit and due date, with every part filled in and read back to the customer

Given the materials, time and running costs for one garment, work out the full cost of the garment and set a price that covers it with a profit, counting materials, your time and running costs, and comparing with the local market
Given your open orders and the hours you can work, plan a week of orders with realistic due dates, taking no more work than your hours allow, with time kept for fittings and busy seasons
Given a week of deposits, payments and spending, record money in and money out in a money book and spot mobile money scams, with the balance correct and never sharing a PIN
Given a finished garment and a phone, make a post or catalogue item that shows the garment, its price and how to order, with a clear photo and no customer's private details shown without permission

lessons.title: Lesson 1: A safe and tidy workshop
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check your workshop for safety risks and fix at least three.
This lesson builds toward: Given your own sewing space, machine and tools, you will check a sewing workshop for safety risks from needles, scissors, irons, electricity and fire, and fix them, finding and fixing at least three risks.
Your hands, eyes and back are your business. An injury can stop your work for weeks, and a fire can burn every customer's fabric. A few habits keep you and your apprentices safe.
Sharp tools: keep fingers away from the needle and use the presser foot; never sew over pins; put scissors, blades and seam rippers in one place, points down; keep needles and pins in a pin cushion or tin, never in your mouth. Throw broken needles into a closed tin, not on the floor where children and customers walk.
Heat and electricity: never leave a hot iron or charcoal iron alone, and stand it where it cannot fall; keep cloth and paper away from it. Check machine and iron cables for cuts and loose plugs. Do not overload one socket with many plugs. Unplug machines and irons when you close. Keep a bucket of sand or water, or a fire extinguisher if you can, near the door.
Your body: sit with your back supported and the table at elbow height, use good light, and stand up and stretch every hour. Keep walkways clear of fabric rolls and cables so nobody trips.
Step by step:
- Walk around your workshop slowly.
- Look for sharp tools, hot irons, damaged cables, overloaded sockets, things to trip on and poor light.
- Write each risk you find.
- Fix three today, for example a pin tin, a safe stand for the iron and clear walkways.
- Teach your apprentices the same rules.
Words to know:
- Presser foot: the part of the sewing machine that holds cloth flat under the needle.
- Overloaded socket: too many plugs in one power point; it can get hot and start a fire.
- Apprentice: a young person learning the trade by working with you.
Try it now: Walk around your workshop now. Write every safety risk you see. Fix three of them today and tick them off your list.
You can now check your workshop for sharp-tool, heat, electrical and trip risks, and fix them.

check.q: Where should you keep pins while you work?
options: In a pin cushion or a tin
In your mouth, so they are quick to reach
On the floor beside your chair
check.why: A cushion or tin keeps pins away from your mouth, the floor and the customer's cloth.

check.q: Five plugs are in one socket and it feels warm. What do you do?
options: Unplug some and spread them out or use a safe extension
Pour water on it to cool it
check.why: A warm, overloaded socket can start a fire; reduce the load and never use water near electricity.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Measurements and the order card
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a customer's measurements and fill in a complete order card.
This lesson builds toward: Given a customer who wants a garment made, you will take the customer's measurements and fill in an order card with style, fabric, price, deposit and due date, with every part filled in and read back to the customer.
Many arguments with customers start because nothing was written down. "I said long sleeves." "You said Friday." "I paid you half." An order card stops this. It is one page or one card for every job, with a copy or photo for the customer.
An order card shows: the customer's name and phone number; the date; the style (a sketch or a photo of the style they want); the measurements; the fabric (who brings it, how many yards or metres, a small cutting stapled on); the price, the deposit paid and the balance; the fitting date and the due date; and your signature and theirs.
Take measurements the same way every time, in the same order, with a good tape measure. Write the unit (cm or inches). Read the measurements and the details back to the customer before they leave. For an aso ebi order in Lagos, a kaba and slit in Kumasi or a boubou in Dakar for Tabaski, the card is the same: the customer and you both know exactly what was agreed.
Step by step:
- Write the customer's name, phone number and the date.
- Sketch the style or attach a photo.
- Measure in your usual order and write the unit.
- Write the fabric details and staple a small cutting.
- Write the price, deposit, balance, fitting date and due date.
- Read it all back, both sign, and give the customer a copy or let them take a photo.
Words to know:
- Order card: a written record of one job: what, for whom, how much and when.
- Deposit: money paid before you start the work.
- Balance: the money still owed after the deposit.
Try it now: Draw your own order card on one page with every part from this lesson. Fill it in for a friend or family member as if they ordered a garment, then read it back to them.
You can now take measurements the same way each time and fill in an order card that you and the customer both agree on.

check.q: A customer says, "You never told me Friday." What would have prevented this?
options: An order card with the due date that you both signed
check.why: A signed card with the due date shows what was agreed.

check.q: You finish measuring. What do you do before the customer leaves?
options: Throw away the scrap of paper
Ask for the full price only
Read every detail back and give them a copy or photo of the card
check.why: Reading back catches mistakes, and a copy means you both hold the same record.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Costing and pricing a garment
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Work out the full cost of one garment and set a price that makes a profit.
This lesson builds toward: Given the materials, time and running costs for one garment, you will work out the full cost of the garment and set a price that covers it with a profit, counting materials, your time and running costs, and comparing with the local market.
Many tailors copy the price of the shop next door. But if your costs are higher, you may be working for nothing. Work out your own cost first, then decide the price.
Materials: everything that goes into the garment if you buy it, such as lining, interfacing, thread, zip, buttons, embroidery thread and packaging. If the customer brings the fabric, do not count the fabric, but count everything else.
Your time: how many hours the garment takes (cutting, sewing, fitting, finishing) times what you want to earn per hour. Running costs: rent, electricity or fuel for the generator, machine repairs, needles, phone data, a share for each garment. A simple way: add up one month's running costs and divide by how many garments you make in a month.
Example (figures are examples only): a woman's dress in Kenya. Materials KES 450, time 4 hours at KES 200 = KES 800, running costs KES 250. Cost = KES 1,500. Add a profit, for example 30%, which is KES 450. Price = KES 1,950. Then compare with the market. If the market price is far lower, look for a cheaper method or a simpler style. Do not just drop your price below cost.
Step by step:
- List and add the materials for one garment.
- Multiply the hours by what you want to earn per hour.
- Add a share of one month's running costs.
- Add the three: that is your cost.
- Add a profit to get your price.
- Compare with the market and adjust the style or method, not just the profit.
Words to know:
- Cost: all the money and time it takes to make one garment.
- Running costs: money you spend to keep the workshop open, like rent and electricity.
- Profit: what is left for you and the business after all costs are paid.
- Margin: the profit you add on top of cost.
Try it now: Choose the garment you make most often. Work out its materials, your time and its share of running costs. Add a profit and write the price. Compare it with what you charge now.
You can now work out what one garment really costs you and set a price that pays you and the business.

check.q: The customer brings her own fabric. What do you still count in materials?
options: Lining, thread, zip and buttons that you buy
check.why: If you buy the lining, thread, zip and buttons, they are your costs even when the fabric is not.

check.q: Materials GHS 60, time GHS 90, running costs GHS 30. What is the cost before profit? (Example figures.)
check.why: 60 + 90 + 30 = 180; profit is added on top of this.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Planning your week and your deadlines
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a week of orders so every due date fits your real hours.
This lesson builds toward: Given your open orders and the hours you can work, you will plan a week of orders with realistic due dates, taking no more work than your hours allow, with time kept for fittings and busy seasons.
The busiest times, such as Christmas, Eid, Tabaski, Easter, school opening and the wedding season, are when tailors lose customers by promising too much. A simple weekly plan helps you say yes only to what you can finish.
First, count your real sewing hours in a week, not counting time for customers, buying materials, power cuts and rest. Next, write how many hours each open order needs (from your costing). Then put each order on a day, earliest due date first, with the fitting before the finishing. Leave about one hour in five free for surprises such as a power cut or a broken machine.
When the week is full, it is full. Offer the next free date, ask for the deposit to hold the slot, or say no politely. In a busy season, set a last day for new orders, for example two weeks before Tabaski in Dakar or before Christmas in Accra, and tell customers early on your status and in the shop.
Step by step:
- Count your real sewing hours this week.
- List open orders with the hours each needs and the due date.
- Place orders on days, earliest due date first, with fittings before finishing.
- Keep about one hour in five free for surprises.
- When the week is full, offer the next free date or say no politely.
Words to know:
- Due date: the day you promised the garment will be ready.
- Fitting: when the customer tries the garment so you can adjust it.
- Last day for orders: the final day you accept new orders before a busy holiday.
Try it now: Write your real sewing hours for next week. List your open orders with the hours each needs and its due date. Put them on days. Is anything late? Decide now what you will tell that customer.
You can now plan a week of orders that fits your hours and set a last day for orders in a busy season.

check.q: You have 30 real sewing hours this week and orders that need 40. What do you do?
options: Move some due dates with the customers now, or take no new orders
check.why: Telling customers early and taking no more than your hours allow keeps your promises and your name.

check.q: Why leave about one hour in five free in your plan?
options: For surprises like power cuts or a broken machine
check.why: Free time absorbs surprises so they do not make orders late.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Money records, mobile money safety and registration
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Record money in and money out for a week and spot mobile money scams.
This lesson builds toward: Given a week of deposits, payments and spending, you will record money in and money out in a money book and spot mobile money scams, with the balance correct and never sharing a PIN.
Keep business money and family money apart. A simple money book has four columns: date, what it was, money in, money out. Write every deposit, balance paid and purchase the same day. At the end of the week, add money in, take away money out, and check the result against the cash and mobile money you really have. In Côte d'Ivoire or Senegal you may write in XOF; in Cameroon in XAF; the method is the same.
Mobile money is fast, and scammers know it. Warning signs: a message saying money was sent to you "by mistake" and asking you to send it back (check your real balance first, and ask your provider to reverse it, never send it yourself); anyone asking for your PIN or a code sent to your phone; a call from a "customer care agent" on a normal number; an urgent big order from a stranger who wants you to pay a "delivery fee" first. A real mobile money provider never asks for your PIN.
Registering your business name can help you open a business bank account, apply for contracts with schools and companies, and look serious to customers. In Kenya, the Business Registration Service handles it through eCitizen; in Nigeria, the Corporate Affairs Commission; in Ghana, the Office of the Registrar of Companies; in Senegal, ask APIX. Rules, steps and fees change, so check the official site or office, and watch for fake agents offering "free registration".
Step by step:
- Open a notebook or phone note with four columns: date, what, in, out.
- Write every deposit, payment and purchase the same day.
- At week's end: total in minus total out.
- Check the result against your real cash and mobile money balance.
- Never share your PIN; check any "wrong send" with your provider before doing anything.
Words to know:
- Money book: a simple record of money coming in and going out.
- PIN: your secret number for mobile money; only you should know it.
- Reversal: when the provider sends back money that went to the wrong person.
- Business name registration: putting your business name on the official government list.
Official sources:
- Business Registration Service (Kenya): business name registration through eCitizen
- Corporate Affairs Commission (Nigeria): business name and company registration
- Office of the Registrar of Companies (Ghana): business names (sole proprietorships)
Try it now: Start your money book today. Write every amount from the last three days that you can remember. Then write the official registry for your country and one thing you will check there.
You can now keep a weekly money book, spot mobile money scams and know which office registers business names in your country.

check.q: A text says KES 5,000 was sent to you by mistake and asks you to send it back. What do you do first?
options: Share your PIN so they can fix it
Check your real balance and contact your provider through its official line
check.why: Many "wrong send" texts are fake; the provider handles real reversals.

check.q: At the end of the week your money book shows more money than you really have. What do you do?
options: Look for a payment or purchase you forgot to write
check.why: A gap usually means something was not written; find it while you still remember.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Showing your work and finding customers
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a post or catalogue item that shows a finished garment, its price and how to order.
This lesson builds toward: Given a finished garment and a phone, you will make a post or catalogue item that shows the garment, its price and how to order, with a clear photo and no customer's private details shown without permission.
Your best advert is your work. A clear photo of a finished garment, shared on WhatsApp status, a WhatsApp Business catalogue, Facebook, Instagram or TikTok, or printed on your shop wall, brings new customers. A designer in Casablanca can show a caftan, and a tailor in Kumasi a kente dress, the same way.
A good photo: daylight, a plain background, the whole garment, then one close-up of the detail or finishing. If a customer is wearing it, ask first if you may share the photo, and never share their name, phone number or measurements. Some customers say no; respect it.
Every post says what it is, a price or "from" price, how long it takes, and how to order (your phone number or "message me"). A price list on the wall or as a picture on your phone helps too: five to ten of your main garments with their prices, based on your costing. Keep data costs low by sharing one good photo instead of many.
Step by step:
- Choose one finished garment.
- Take a photo in daylight on a plain background, plus one close-up.
- Ask permission if a customer is in the photo.
- Write what it is, the price, how long it takes and how to order.
- Post it, or add it to your catalogue or price list.
Words to know:
- Catalogue: a list of your products with photos and prices, for example in WhatsApp Business.
- Price list: a list of your main garments and what each one costs to order.
- Permission: the customer saying yes before you share their photo.
Try it now: Take a photo of one finished garment in daylight. Write a post with what it is, the price from your costing, how long it takes and how to order. Share it on your status or save it for your catalogue.
You can now show your work with a clear photo, a price and how to order, while protecting your customers' privacy.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Safe workshop No safety risks listed, or risks listed but none fixed. At least three risks found and fixed, such as a pin tin, a safe iron stand and clear walkways. All risks listed and fixed, and apprentices taught the rules. Order card The card misses the price, deposit, balance or due date. The card has style, measurements with units, fabric, price, deposit, balance, fitting and due date, and space for both signatures. Used with a real customer, read back and shared as a copy or photo. Costed price list Prices are copied or guessed, with no cost worked out. At least five garments, each with materials, time and running costs worked out and a price above cost. Each price is also compared with the local market, with a note on what to change if it is too high. Weekly plan The plan has more hours of work than hours available, or no due dates. Orders placed by due date within real hours, with fittings before finishing and some time kept free. Includes a last day for orders in the next busy season and how customers will be told. Money book No record, or business and family money mixed. A week of deposits, payments and spending with a correct balance, and the PIN rule written down. The balance is checked against real cash and mobile money, and the registry for the learner's country is noted. Showing the work No photo, or a photo with no price or way to order. A clear daylight photo with what it is, price, time and how to order, and no customer's private details. Added to a catalogue or price list, with permission recorded for any customer in the photo. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What must a post about your garment include?
options: The price you paid for thread
What it is, a price, how long it takes and how to order
check.why: Customers need to know what it is, what it costs, when they can have it and how to order.

check.q: You want to share a photo of a customer wearing your dress. What do you do?
options: Ask her first, and share no name or phone number
Post it with her name so people can ask her
Post it; she is your customer
check.why: A customer's photo and details are hers; ask first and keep private details out.
